paragraphs: “Blast it all!” Ivan cried, his face working with anger. “Why are you always so scared for your life? Dmitri’s threats are only things he says in a temper. They mean nothing. He won’t kill you—you’re not the one he’ll kill!”
“Me first of all. He’d squash me like a fly. But what I’m even more afraid of is being taken for his accomplice when he does something mad to his father.”
“Why would anyone take you for an accomplice?”
“They’ll think I’m his accomplice because I gave him the signals, and they were a great secret.”
“What signals? Who did you give them to? Confound you, say it plainly.”

“I have to admit,” Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic composure, “that Fyodor Pavlovitch and I share a secret in this matter. You know yourself (if you do know it) that for some days now he has been locking himself in the moment night falls, or even the evening. Lately you’ve gone up to your room early each evening, and yesterday you never came down at all. So perhaps you don’t know how carefully he now locks himself in. Even when Grigory Vassilyevitch comes to the door, he won’t open until he hears his voice. But Grigory Vassilyevitch doesn’t come, because I’m now the only one who attends him in his room. That’s how he arranged it himself, from the time this business with Agrafena Alexandrovna started. At night, though, on his orders, I go off to the lodge. So I can’t sleep before midnight. I stay on watch instead, getting up and walking around the yard, waiting for Agrafena Alexandrovna to arrive. These last few days he has been simply frantic waiting for her. His argument is that she is afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya, as he calls him), ‘and so,’ says he, ‘she’ll come to me by the back way, late at night. You watch out for her,’ says he, ‘until midnight and after. If she does come, run up and knock on my door, or on the window from the garden. Knock twice to begin with, fairly gently, then three more times, quicker. Then,’ says he, ‘I’ll know at once that she’s here, and I’ll open the door to you quietly.’ He gave me a second signal in case something unexpected happens. First two knocks, then a pause, then another, much louder. Then he’ll understand that something has suddenly come up and that I need to see him, and he’ll open up so I can go in and talk to him. That’s for the case where Agrafena Alexandrovna can’t come herself but sends word. Dmitri Fyodorovitch might come as well, you see, so I have to tell him he’s near. His honor is dreadfully afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had come and were shut in with him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch turned up anywhere nearby, I’d be obliged to warn him at once by knocking three times. So the first signal, five knocks, means Agrafena Alexandrovna has come, and the second, three knocks, means ‘something important to tell you.’ His honor has shown them to me several times and explained them. Since nobody in the whole world knows these signals except me and his honor, he would open the door without the slightest hesitation and without calling out (he’s dreadfully afraid of calling out loud). Well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows those signals now too.”
“How does he know them? Did you tell him? How did you dare?”

“Fear made me do it. How could I dare hold it back from him? Every day Dmitri Fyodorovitch kept at me: ‘You’re deceiving me, you’re hiding something from me! I’ll break both your legs.’ So I told him the secret signals, to show him my slavish devotion and to satisfy him that I wasn’t deceiving him and was telling him everything I could.”
“If you think he’ll use those signals and try to get in, then don’t let him in.”
“But if I’m down with a fit, how am I supposed to stop him then? And even if I weren’t, would I dare, knowing how desperate he is?”
“Blast it! What makes you so certain you’re going to have a fit, damn you? Are you laughing at me?”
“How would I dare laugh at you? I’m not in the mood for laughing, with this fear on me. I feel a fit coming. I have a foreboding of it. The fright alone will bring it on.”
“Damn it! If you’re laid up, Grigory will be keeping watch. Tell Grigory ahead of time, and he’ll certainly keep him out.”

“I would never dare tell Grigory Vassilyevitch about the signals unless my master ordered it. As for Grigory Vassilyevitch hearing him and refusing to let him in, he has been unwell since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna plans to give him a remedy tomorrow. They’ve only just agreed on it. It’s a very odd remedy of hers. Marfa Ignatyevna knows of a preparation and keeps it by her always. It’s a strong brew made from some herb. The secret of it is hers, and she gives it to Grigory Vassilyevitch three times a year, whenever his lumbago is so bad that he can hardly move. Then she takes a towel, soaks it in the stuff, and rubs his whole back for half an hour until it is quite red and swollen. Whatever is left in the bottle she gives him to drink, with a special prayer. Not every drop, though, because on those occasions she keeps some back and drinks it herself. And since neither of them ever touches strong drink, I assure you they both fall asleep at once and sleep soundly for a very long time. When Grigory Vassilyevitch wakes, he’s perfectly well, but Marfa Ignatyevna always has a headache from it. So if Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her plan tomorrow, they’ll hear nothing and won’t get in Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s way. They’ll be asleep.”

“What a rigmarole! And it all falls together at once, as if it were planned. You’ll have your fit and the two of them will be out cold,” cried Ivan. “Aren’t you arranging it that way?” he burst out suddenly, frowning menacingly.
“How could I?... And why would I, when everything depends on Dmitri Fyodorovitch and what he plans?... If he means to do something, he’ll do it. If not, I’m not the one pushing him at his father.”

“And why would he go to father at all, least of all sneaking in, if Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t coming, as you say yourself?” Ivan went on, going white with anger. “You say so yourself, and the whole time I’ve been here I’ve been sure it was all the old man’s delusion and that the creature won’t come to him. Why would Dmitri burst in on him if she doesn’t come? Speak up, I want to know what you’re thinking!”

“You know yourself why he’ll come. What does it matter what I think? His honor will come simply because he’s in a rage, or perhaps because my illness makes him suspicious. He’ll rush in, as he did yesterday, too impatient to wait, to search the rooms and see whether she’s slipped past him in secret. He also knows perfectly well that Fyodor Pavlovitch keeps a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied with ribbon and sealed with three seals. In his own hand it says, ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come,’ and three days later he added, ‘for my little chicken.’ Who knows what that might lead to?”

“Nonsense!” cried Ivan, nearly beside himself. “Dmitri won’t come to rob anyone, or to kill my father for the money. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, the frantic, savage fool, but he won’t steal.”

“He needs money very badly now—more badly than ever, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You don’t know how badly,” Smerdyakov explained, with perfect composure and remarkable distinctness. “He counts that three thousand as his own, too. He told me so himself. ‘My father still owes me exactly three thousand,’ he said. And there’s something else, Ivan Fyodorovitch, which is perfectly true, so consider it. It’s nearly certain, so to speak, that Agrafena Alexandrovna could make him marry her, if she cared to—the master himself, I mean, Fyodor Pavlovitch—and of course she may care to. All I’ve said is that she won’t come, but maybe she’s aiming higher, I mean to be mistress here. I know myself that Samsonov, her merchant, laughed about it with her and told her quite openly it wouldn’t be a stupid thing at all. And she has plenty of sense. She wouldn’t marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So, taking that into account, Ivan Fyodorovitch, think what follows: neither Dmitri Fyodorovitch, nor you, nor your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch would get anything after the master’s death, not one rouble, because Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him just to get her hands on all of it, every bit of the money. But if your father were to die now, there would certainly be some forty thousand, even for Dmitri Fyodorovitch, whom he hates so, because he has left no will.... Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows all that very well.”
Ivan’s face shuddered for a moment, and he flushed all at once.
“Then why on earth,” he cut in suddenly, “are you advising me to go to Tchermashnya? What did you mean by it? If I go away, you can see what will happen here.” Ivan could hardly get his breath.
“Precisely so,” said Smerdyakov, quietly and sensibly, but keeping his eyes on Ivan.
“What do you mean, ‘precisely so’?” Ivan asked, a menacing light in his eyes, holding himself in with difficulty.

“I spoke out of pity for you. In your place I’d simply drop the whole thing ... before I’d stay on in a position like this,” Smerdyakov answered, meeting Ivan’s blazing eyes with the most open look. Neither said anything.

“You’re a complete idiot, it seems, and what’s more ... a downright scoundrel.” Ivan stood up abruptly from the bench. He was about to walk straight out the gate, but stopped short and turned back to Smerdyakov. Then something strange happened. In a sudden fit, Ivan bit his lip and clenched his fists, and a moment more would have thrown himself at Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov saw it in the same instant, flinched and shrank back. But the moment went by without harm to him, and Ivan turned silently toward the gate, seemingly bewildered.
“I’m going to Moscow tomorrow, if you want to know—early tomorrow morning. That’s all!” he said suddenly, aloud and angrily. Later he himself wondered why he had needed to say it to Smerdyakov then.
“That’s the very best thing you can do,” he responded, as if he had been expecting to hear it; “only you can always be sent for by telegram from Moscow, if anything happens here.”

Ivan stopped again and turned sharply back to Smerdyakov. But a change had taken place in him too. All his easy familiarity and carelessness had vanished. His face showed attention and expectancy, eager yet timid and cringing.
“Haven’t you something more to say—something to add?” you could read in the intent look he fixed on Ivan.
“And couldn’t I be sent for from Tchermashnya as well—if something happened?” Ivan suddenly shouted, raising his voice for no reason he knew.
“From Tchermashnya as well ... yes, you could be sent for,” Smerdyakov muttered, almost whispering, looking thrown off balance but staring hard into Ivan’s eyes.
“Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is closer. Do you insist on Tchermashnya to save me the cost of the fare, or to save me going so far out of my way?”

“Precisely so ...” Smerdyakov muttered, his voice breaking. He looked at Ivan with a revolting smile and prepared once more to draw back. But to his astonishment Ivan burst out laughing and went through the gate still laughing. Anyone who saw his face then would have known he wasn’t laughing from a light heart; nor could he himself have said what he felt at that moment. His movements and his walk were those of a man in a nervous frenzy.
